title: How To Ask For And Receive Your Students’ Attention Within Two Seconds ttention-within-two-seconds/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a five-step method for teaching students to respond to a call for attention almost instantly. He recommends first explaining why fast attention matters, then choosing a simple spoken signal — he favors the teacher's own voice, such as "Can I have your attention please," over bells or whistles, since it builds the broader habit of listening whenever the teacher speaks. The core discipline is expecting an immediate response from the very first practice, since any leniency causes response time to creep longer and longer over time. He details modeling the desired behavior explicitly, including how not to do it, and making practice fun with silly filler phrases students say while pretending to work before the signal is given. He closes by emphasizing that this single routine, once mastered, saves enormous time and underpins many other areas of classroom management.
points: A five-step method — explain why, choose a signal, expect immediate response, model it, make practice fun — teaches near-instant response to attention calls.
The teacher's own voice (e.g., "Can I have your attention please") is recommended over bells or whistles, since it builds a broader habit of listening whenever the teacher speaks.
Expecting an immediate response from the very first practice is critical — any leniency causes response time to creep longer over time.
Practice sessions are made fun with silly filler phrases ("blah, blah, blah") that students say while pretending to work before the signal is given.
quotes: The ability to ask for and receive your students’ attention is crucial.
This underscores the importance of selling not just your lessons, but anything and everything you want your students to be able to do well.
The biggest mistake teachers make is allowing students more time than they need to respond. This is key.
Your students need to see exactly what giving you their attention looks like.
In the past, I’ve used “hey, hey, whaddya say,” “murmur, murmur,” and “blah, blah, blah,” as well as a few others. The goofier, the better.
It saves loads of time, improves listening , encourages group responsibility, and allows you to have instant and total control of your class anytime you need it.
